```{r, include = FALSE}
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(knitr)
library(mizer)
library(mizerExperimental)
library(mizerReef)

data(caribbean_3_model)
params <- caribbean_3_model
gear_params(params)["inverts, knife_edge_gear", "catchability"] <- 0
params@other_params$include_sen_mort <- TRUE
```

\newpage

# Model Description

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
[Skip to Resources](#resources)
:::

`caribbean_3_model` reproduces the three-group trait-based reef model from
@Rogers_2018 -- predators, herbivores, and a general group of benthic
invertebrates -- inside mizerReef. It is deliberately coarse: useful when a
species-group resolution is enough, or as a minimal starting point for
setting up a new reef model, before working up to something like the
[10-group Karpata Reef model](karpata_model-description.html), which
parameterises the same three broad functional groups against finer field
data. This page documents this model's specific parameters and how they were
tuned; for the general mizerReef formulation these parameters plug into, see
`vignette("model-description")`.

Biomass estimates were based on data collected from relatively un-fished
reefs within a marine reserve in Bonaire. This data was part of the FORCE
dataset that categorised fish community structure and habitat complexity
across Caribbean coral reefs [@Dryden2016; @Rogers_2014; @Newman_2015;
@Williams_2015; @Williams_2016]. A marine-reserve site was chosen
deliberately, for this model and for the 10-group Karpata Reef model alike,
so that observed biomasses would not need to be corrected for fishing
pressure before being used to calibrate the models. Visual surveys recorded
fish up to 5 cm in length. The cutoff weight for observed biomass estimates
was calculated using published length-weight relationships [@FishBase]. The
cutoff size is given in the table below along with the observed biomass per
square meter in grams.

```{r, echo = FALSE}
params@species_params %>%
    filter(!is.na(biomass_observed)) %>%
    select(species,biomass_observed, biomass_cutoff) %>%
    kable(row.names = FALSE,
          col.names = c("Species Group",
                        "Observed Biomass [g/m^2]", "Cutoff Size [g]"))
```

## Interaction matrix

The $\theta_{ij}$ matrix sets the interaction strength between predator group
$i$ and prey group $j$, where 0 means the groups cannot interact. Only
predators eat other groups. Their interaction strengths were calibrated so
that adult predators' diet is 33% predators, 17% herbivores and 50%
invertebrates, the proportions used by @Rogers_2018. The herbivore value is
above 1 because most herbivores of the size predators prefer are hiding in
refuge.

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 3.5, fig.width = 5, fig.cap = "Interaction strength between each predator group (rows) and prey group (columns). Predators consume all three groups, at different strengths; herbivores and invertebrates do not prey on fish."}
ggplot(melt(params@interaction),
       aes(x = prey, y = reorder(predator, desc(predator)), fill = value)) +
    geom_tile(colour = "black", linewidth = 0.25) +
    scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", high = "blue",
                        limit = c(0, max(params@interaction)),
                        guide = "legend") +
    labs(y = "Predator", x = "Prey", fill = "Interaction") +
    scale_x_discrete(labels = c("Predators","Herbivores", "Inverts")) +
    scale_y_discrete(labels = c("Inverts","Herbivores", "Predators")) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, vjust = 1, hjust = 1))
```

## Predation kernel

The parameters for the predation kernels were based on the global average
predator-prey mass ratio for marine organisms and home range size estimates
from @Nash_2014. All estimates fall within observed ranges. All groups use a
lognormal predation kernel with the same parameters as in @Rogers_2014.

```{r, echo = FALSE, results='asis'}
params@species_params %>%
    filter(pred_kernel_type == "lognormal") %>%
    select(beta, sigma, gamma) %>%
    kable()
```

## Vulnerability to predation

```{r, include = FALSE}
refuge_params <- params@other_params$refuge_params
```

This model uses the `r params@other_params$refuge_params$method`
refuge method (see `vignette("model-description")`'s
[refuge profiles](model-description.html#refuge-profiles) section for the
general formulation and @Rogers_2018 for its derivation). All fish are
assumed to utilize refuge ($\tau = 1$). Fish smaller than
`r paste(refuge_params$w_settle,"g")` are assumed to be larval reef fish that
have not yet settled to the reef. A maximum proportion of
`r paste(100*refuge_params$max_protect,"%")` of fish are protected at any
given time. In this model holes outnumber fish, so fish between 2.5 and
20 cm long are protected at that maximum.

<details>
<summary>Refuge length bins and densities used in the steady state (same Bonaire FORCE data as the 10-group model)</summary>

The following table gives the fish length bins and refuge densities that
define the refuge profile used in the steady state. Length bins and refuge
densities were garnered from the FORCE data in the same location as biomass
estimates -- the same [`karpata_refuge`](../reference/karpata_refuge.html)
profile used by the 10-group model.

```{r, echo = FALSE}
params@other_params$refuge_params$method_params %>%
    mutate(refuge_density = round(refuge_density,3)) %>%
    kable(row.names = FALSE,
          col.names = c("Start of Bin (cm)",
                        "End of Bin (cm)",
                        "Refuge Density (no./m^2)"))
```

</details>

<details>
<summary>How each species group interacts with predation refuge</summary>

Each species group can utilise benthic structures differently depending on
their specific traits.

```{r, echo = FALSE, results='asis'}
params@species_params %>%
    select(refuge_user, blocked_pred) %>%
    mutate(refuge_user  = case_when(refuge_user == TRUE ~ 'Yes',
                                    refuge_user == FALSE ~ '×')) %>%
    mutate(blocked_pred = case_when(blocked_pred == TRUE ~ '×',
                                    blocked_pred == FALSE ~ 'Yes')) %>%
    kable(col.names = c("Group", "Uses refuge?", "Accesses prey in refuge?"))
```

</details>

The figure below shows the density-dependent refuge profile produced by the
competitive method at steady state. Invertebrates are not shown as they do
not use refuge (`refuge_user = FALSE`, see the table above).

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 3, fig.width = 7, fig.cap = "Proportion of each refuge-using group protected from predation, by body length, at steady state."}
plotRefugeProfile(params)
```

\newpage

## Consumption

Consumption of the detrital and algal resources is subject to a Holling type
II functional response (see `vignette("model-description")`'s
[Consumption and satiation](model-description.html#consumption-and-satiation)
section for the general formula). The parameter $h$ is the max consumption
rate for a consumer of size 1 gram, chosen so that consumers subject to
satiation are neither too starved nor totally satiated; $\alpha_i$ is the
proportion of consumed biomass retained, with $1-\alpha_i$ expelled as
faeces, which contribute to detritus.

No maximum consumption rate is imposed for predators. Herbivores are subject
to satiation here, unlike the package default for herbivorous groups: without
it, herbivores eating the algae production used here mature in under half a
year. The realised feeding level for herbivores is close to 1, consistent
with Caribbean herbivores' guts being observed to be full essentially
continuously [@Ferreira1998; @Kopp2010] -- the citations behind the
package's herbivore-satiation default describe grazing *pressure on the
shared algae resource* not self-regulating when food is abundant, which is
unaffected by this change (see [the main model description's Algae
section](model-description.html#algae)).

```{r, echo = FALSE}
params@species_params %>%
    filter(satiation == TRUE) %>%
    select(h, alpha, n) %>%
    kable()
```

### Metabolic losses

Standard metabolism occurs at rate $k_{s.i}$; losses due to activity and
movement occur at rate $k_i$ (see `vignette("model-description")` for the
general growth/reproduction formulation).

```{r, results='asis', echo = FALSE}
params@species_params %>%
    select(ks, p, k) %>%
    kable()
```

### Maturation and growth

Maturation length and age data were based on the most commonly observed
species from each functional group in the FORCE data set [@Dryden2016;
@Rogers_2014; @Newman_2015; @Williams_2015; @Williams_2016]. For predators,
this was the graysby grouper, *Cephalopholis cruentata*. The most commonly
observed herbivore was the stoplight parrotfish, *Sparisoma viride*. Relevant
maturity parameters were pulled from FishBase [@FishBase].

Both species are protogynous hermaphrodites, so first (female) maturity and
the later change from female to male are easy to confuse. The `age_mat`
values below are the age at first maturity for both species, 2 years, from
FishBase; earlier versions of this model used the age at sex change for
predators (4 years) and other estimates for herbivores (4 and 1.6 years).
`w_mat` is the weight at 16 cm, FishBase's length at 50% maturity for both
species. In the steady state, predators mature at
`r round(age_mat(params)[["predators"]], 1)` years and herbivores at
`r round(age_mat(params)[["herbivores"]], 1)` years.

```{r, echo = FALSE}
params@species_params %>%
    select(w_mat, w_max, age_mat) %>%
    kable()
```

The model's growth was calibrated to the age at maturity, not to a whole
growth curve, so it does not follow the von Bertalanffy curve given by
`k_vb` below (compare with `plotGrowthCurves(params)`); $a$ and $b$ are the
allometric weight-length parameters $w = a l^b$ ($w$ in grams, $l$ in
centimetres), taken from the literature.

```{r, echo = FALSE}
params@species_params %>%
    select(k_vb, w_max, a, b) %>%
    kable()
```

## Mortality {#mortality}

See `vignette("model-description")`'s [Mortality](model-description.html#mortality)
section for the general formulation. This model's residual-natural- and
senescence-mortality parameters:

```{r, results = 'asis', echo = FALSE}
ext_mort <- params@other_params[['ext_mort_params']]
```

We use a residual natural mortality rate of $\mu_{nat} =$
`r ext_mort$nat_mort` per year at size 1 gram, and senescence mortality
parameters $k_{sen} =$ `r ext_mort$sen_prop` (`sen_prop`) and $p_{sen} =$
`r ext_mort$sen_curve` (`sen_curve`, the exponent governing how steeply
mortality climbs as individuals approach their maximum size), both based on
estimates from @Hatcher_1988.

### Fishing mortality

Fishing parameters for mizerReef models can be set up with `setFishing()`.
The vignettes were run with the following fishing parameters:

```{r, echo = FALSE}
params@gear_params %>%
    filter(catchability > 0) %>%
    select(species, knife_edge_size, catchability) %>%
    kable(row.names = FALSE,
          col.names = c("Group", "Minimum fishing size [g]",
                        "Catchability [1/year]"))
```

## Reproduction {#reproduction}

The reproduction parameters $\epsilon_i$ and $R_{max.i}$ are not directly
observable. Their values were instead chosen so as to produce steady-state
abundances of the groups that are in line with observations and to give
reasonable values for the reproduction level -- the ratio between the actual
reproduction rate $R_i$ and the maximal possible reproduction rate
$R_{\max.i}$. Herbivore reproduction was also tuned to give about 10
juveniles (0.03-1.6 g) per square metre, as in @Rogers_2018. Fish start life
at $w_{min} = 10^{-1.5}$ g, the smallest fish size in @Rogers_2018.

```{r, echo = FALSE}
df <- params@species_params
df %>%
    select(w_min, erepro, R_max) %>%
    kable()
```

# Resources {#resources}

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
[Skip to Tuning the Steady State](#tuning-the-steady-state)
:::

The fish spectrum is fed by three background resources: plankton, algae, and
detritus. As in @Rogers_2018, only predators feed on plankton (when small),
herbivores feed only on algae, and invertebrates only on detritus. See
`vignette("model-description")`'s [unstructured resource
dynamics](model-description.html#unstructured-resource-dynamics) section for
the general formulation and its relationship to mizerShelf.

### Plankton {#plankton}
```{r, echo = FALSE}
wcutoff <- params@resource_params$w_pp_cutoff
lambda <- params@resource_params$lambda
kappa <- params@resource_params$kappa
```

The plankton spectrum ranges from $w_0=`r signif(min(params@w_full), digits = 1)`$
to $w_{cutoff}=`r wcutoff`$ grams. The steady state abundance of plankton at
size 1 gram is $\kappa=`r signif(kappa, digits = 3)` (g/m^{2})$, with slope
$\lambda=`r signif(lambda, digits = 3)`$.

### Algae {#algae}
The algal resource is described only by its total biomass $B_A$, and feeding
on it is not size-based. In the steady state the total algal biomass per
square meter is $B_A = `r signif(algae_biomass(params), digits = 3)`$ grams.
Herbivores' interaction with algae was chosen to give a standing biomass of
350 g/m^2, the midpoint of a 150-550 g/m^2 range (a Caribbean estimate of 10-100 g dry
weight per m^2, converted with an assumed wet:dry ratio of 5-10).

Algae has a carrying capacity of
$K_A = `r signif(params@other_params$algae$capacity, digits = 4)`$ g/m^2
(see the main model description's [carrying-capacity
variant](model-description.html#carrying-capacity-variant)), so algae cannot
grow without limit if grazing falls, for example on a degraded reef.
Detritus has no carrying capacity.

```{r, echo = FALSE}
params@species_params %>%
    select(rho_algae, interaction_algae) %>%
    rename(rho = rho_algae) %>%
    filter(rho > 0) %>%
    kable()
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, include=FALSE}
pA <- params@other_params$algae$growth
```

Algal *production* -- a fixed, literature-informed constant, `algae_growth_initial`
in `setAlgaeParams()` -- is `r signif(pA,digits = 4)` grams per square meter
per year at steady state. Note this value is not retuned to match
consumption the way detritus production is (see below); see
`vignette("model-description")`'s Algae section for why.

### Detritus
Detritus is consumed by benthic invertebrates, also not size-based. In the
steady state the total detrital biomass per square meter is
$B_D = `r signif(detritus_biomass(params), digits = 4)`$ grams.
Invertebrates' interaction with detritus was chosen to give a detritus
lifetime of 3.85 hours, the midpoint of the 2.8-4.9 hour residence time of benthic detritus measured
at Palmyra Atoll (Max et al. 2013, *Mar. Ecol. Prog. Ser.* 482: 181-195).

```{r, echo = FALSE}
params@species_params %>%
    select(rho_detritus,interaction_detritus) %>%
    rename(rho = rho_detritus) %>%
    filter(rho > 0) %>%
    kable()
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
#| include: false
e_d <- params@other_params$detritus$ext_decomp
s_d <- params@other_params$detritus$sen_decomp
r <- getDetritusProduction(params)
pf <- r[1]
pd <- r[2]
dext <- params@other_params$detritus$external
```
Detritus production comes from three sources: defecation, decomposing dead
organisms, and external input. At steady state, decomposing dead organisms
contribute `r paste(round(pd,2))` g/year and defecation contributes
`r paste(round(pf,2))` g/year -- `r paste(100*e_d,"%")` of external mortality
and `r paste(100*s_d,"%")` of senescence mortality is assumed to decompose to
detritus (estimates from @Hatcher_1988). The remaining external-input term is
solved for so that, unlike algae, detritus *production* matches current
consumption: at steady state it is `r paste(round(dext,2))` g/year. Where
this is negative, faeces and mortality alone already produce more detritus
than is consumed, and the excess is assumed to be washed away.

# Tuning the Steady State

The parameter tables (`caribbean_3_species`, `caribbean_3_interaction`)
already hold the calibrated values, so the model is rebuilt from scratch by a
short script: it reads the tables, sets up the model with `newReefParams()`,
and projects it forward until it settles at steady state (see
`inst/scripts/caribbean-3-calibration-clean.r` in the package source).

The values were found once, by a search that adjusted seven parameters (the
predators' three interaction strengths, the reproduction of each group, and
plankton abundance) until the steady state matched seven targets: the three
observed biomasses, about 10 herbivore juveniles per m^2, the 33% and 17%
shares of predators and herbivores in adult predators' diet, and predators
maturing at age 2. That search does not need to be repeated to use or
rebuild the model. For how to calibrate a new model, see
`vignette("steady-state-recipe")`.

<details>
<summary>Show the script that builds the model</summary>

```{r, echo = TRUE, eval = FALSE, code = readLines(system.file("scripts", "caribbean-3-calibration-clean.r", package = "mizerReef"))}
```

</details>
